The "Coterie" extends many thanks to the citizens of Savoy and her brother societies for liberal contributions to her library fund.

While the "Coterie" does not hope to add lustre to its roll of fame this year by the woman whose "nom-deplume" it has chosen for a name, yet it does hope to add some impetus to the onward march of truth.

From a note of regret for lost members appearing in a Messenger it appears that many young ladies withdrew from the Platonian Society when they joined the Philomathean, as well as when they joined the Coterie and other organization societies. As only fifteen members are in the photograph of the Coterie (taken in this chapter) for 1885-1886, there is the suggestion that the membership may have had limited purposes. The society had a distinctive dress uniform, as one member relates, "to show their importance."

Mrs. Lee De Jarnet⁷⁰ gives the following description:

The material was cotton, the color selected was blue, but there were several shades of blue in it. The uniform consisted of navy blue skirts with a white waist, the front of the basque (believe it or not). There were groups of books (could have been tarletan), and finished with a ruffle on the bottom. We really did feel important in that uniform and we walked ahead of those who were not in the Coterie. These were the times when our wardrobe of school frocks ran low and the uniform was a welcome sight, indeed.

On the eve of Christmas in that busy year of 1885 the three societies held a public meeting on the campus of some note.
